title: The gates of tears (Berakhot 32b)
hook: since the Temple fell the gates of prayer may be locked, but the gates of tears are never locked
tomorrow: a snake bites him in the middle of prayer. why doesn't he stop?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses wouldn't let go: hold on and plead. Today the week comes back, with one more door that stays open.

Some people can't cry at the sad part of a movie, then cry at a commercial a week later. Tears keep their own schedule. Rabbi Elazar says something hard: since the day the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer have been locked. So what's left? He finishes the thought. Even though the gates of prayer are locked, the gates of tears are not.
screen: `TEARS KEEP THEIR OWN SCHEDULE.` → `THE GATES OF PRAYER, LOCKED.` → `THE GATES OF TEARS, OPEN.`

segments.voice: He brings a verse for each gate. For the locked one, Lamentations: "Also when I cry and shout, he shutteth out my prayer." For the open one, a psalm: "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear unto my cry; hold not thy peace at my tears." Words can feel like they're hitting a closed door. Tears, Rabbi Elazar says, still get through. Now look at where this lands, at the end of the week. Yochanan ben Zakkai wept and said, I don't know. Set words needed something new each time. The early pious prepared their hearts before a word was said. Hannah whispered, then made a bold case. Moses grabbed hold and pleaded for others. Tears are where all of that goes when the words run out. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight. In this teaching, crying isn't a failure to pray. It may be the prayer that still gets in.
screen: `LAMENTATIONS: HE SHUTS OUT MY PRAYER.` · `THE PSALM: HOLD NOT THY PEACE AT MY TEARS.` · `THE WEEK, WHEN WORDS RUN OUT.` · `CRYING ISN'T A FAILURE.` · then, large: `THE GATES OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands open on your knees, palms up. Let whatever is close to the surface come up, without pushing it down or forcing it. If something wells up, let it; if nothing does, the open hands are enough.
screen: `HANDS OPEN, PALMS UP.` · `LET IT COME, OR NOT.` · `OPEN HANDS ARE ENOUGH.`

howItsDone: Jewish prayer has long made room for tears, from the psalms to the High Holy Day services, and Rabbi Elazar's saying about the gates of tears is often quoted to comfort people who find it hard to pray in words.
